steps.title: Prepare computational environment
steps.instruction: Install MATLAB R2025a on a workstation equipped with an Intel Core i7‑6700HQ CPU (2.6 GHz), 16 GB RAM, 64‑bit Windows 11, and an NVIDIA GTX 950 GPU.

steps.title: Collect leaf image dataset
steps.instruction: Gather RGB images of grapevine leaves representing the four classes (Leaf Blight, Black Rot, Esca, Healthy). Ensure images include real‑world variations such as shadows, overlapping leaves, and background clutter.

steps.title: Segment and pad images
steps.instruction: Apply a segmentation routine to isolate leaf/disease regions and remove background. Use reflection padding so that each image can be tiled completely by 16 × 16‑pixel blocks without discontinuities at the borders.

steps.title: Divide images into blocks
steps.instruction: Split each padded image into non‑overlapping blocks of 16 × 16 pixels.

steps.title: Compute (q,τ)‑NC‑QD features
steps.instruction: For every pixel x in each block, evaluate the fractional (q,τ)‑nabla operator (Eq. 3) with parameters α = 0.8, q = 0.5, τ = 1.2 to obtain a feature value. Store the resulting feature map for the block.

steps.title: Reduce feature dimensionality
steps.instruction: For the feature values of each block, calculate the four statistical descriptors: mean, variance, skewness, and kurtosis. Concatenate these four numbers to form the reduced feature vector for that block.

steps.title: Assemble image‑level feature set
steps.instruction: Append the reduced feature vectors of all blocks belonging to the same image into a single feature vector representing that image. Collect the vectors of all images into the final feature matrix.

steps.title: Tune (q,τ) parameters (optional)
steps.instruction: If desired, repeat steps 4‑6 while varying τ (0.5 → 1.2), q (lower values) and α (around 0.8) to observe classification accuracy. The study found the optimal configuration α = 0.8, q = 0.5, τ = 1.2 giving 93.89 % accuracy for the handcrafted feature extractor.

description: Plant disease detection for quantitative plant physiology analysis has become simpler thanks to developments in computer vision and imaging, which is a positive step toward sustainable agriculture and food security. Due to their economic significance, grapevine diseases are receiving more attention in recent research that has investigated a variety of machine learning approaches for plant disease detection. Traditionally, methods like Local Binary Patterns (LBP) [7], Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG), and Gray-Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) are used to extract handcrafted features like color, texture, and shape [3]. Although somewhat successful, these approaches have trouble handling the intricate differences in how diseases manifest. On the other hand, by automatically extracting features from images, Deep Learning (DL) models in particular, Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) performed better. Researchers have used architectures like AlexNet, VGG16, and ResNet to classify grapevine leaves with encouraging accuracy [8]. Nevertheless, CNNs frequently need a lot of data and a lot of processing power. Ferentinos et al., [8] (2018) proposed a DL approach for plant disease detection using CNNs architectures (AlexNet, GoogLeNet), including grapevine diseases. The model achieved up to 99.5 % accuracy on test sets. The significance of this study was to demonstrate the power of DL on plant pathology. However, some classes had many samples, while others had relatively few which can bias the model toward limiting its generalization to rare or early-stage infections. In their study,Amara et al [9] proposed disease classification method for grapevine and tomato. This study applied pretrained AlexNet and GoogleNet and achieved over 96 % accuracy on grape leaf disease detection. The significance of this study was that it reduces the need for large datasets.
